context: Dante first loved her as a boy in Florence. Now she warms his mind with truth, as she has just done in explaining the moon.

note: The method of the medieval schools, which Beatrice followed in Canto 2: first knock down the wrong answer, then prove the right one.

The souls in the moon look like faint reflections in glass or shallow water. They are the last in whom Dante can make out human features. In the higher heavens the blessed are hidden in their own light.

quote: a white pearl upon a forehead
note: In Dante's Italian the forehead is the white thing: a pearl worn on a pale brow, white on white, hard to make out. Ladies of his day wore pearls this way.

quote: fell in love with his own reflection
note: Narcissus, the youth in Ovid's Metamorphoses (book 3) who saw his face in a pool and took it for a real person. Dante does the reverse: he takes real persons for reflections, and turns to look behind him.
Not literally. Canto 4 explains that all the blessed live in the highest heaven, and only show themselves in the moon as a sign of their rank that Dante can grasp.

quote: the true light that gives them peace
note: God. Souls who see him cannot stray from the truth, so Dante may believe whatever they tell him.
Heaven is pictured throughout as the court of a king. God wants all his courtiers to be as generous in love as he is.
A nun.
Blessedness has made her more beautiful than she was in life, which is why Dante did not know her at once.

context: The first soul Dante speaks with in Heaven. Her brother Forese told him in Purgatorio 24 that she was already here.
The moon's sphere is the smallest, nearest the earth at the center, and so it turns most slowly.

note: The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, understood as the love of God. These souls want only what that love wants.

The reward fits the soul. The moon changes its face through the month, and those who appear in it had wills that gave way under pressure. Theirs is the lowest degree of bliss, but it is bliss, with no regret in it.

quote: do you desire a higher station
note: The question the canto exists to answer: if some of the blessed are nearer to God than others, how can the lower ones be perfectly happy?
Read two ways: like a girl glowing with first love, or burning in the fire of the first Love, which is God.
Dante's word is carità, charity: the love of God, and of others for God's sake. Theology counted it the greatest of the virtues.
To love is to want what the beloved wants. A soul that loves God cannot wish for a place other than the one God has given it.

"E 'n la sua volontade è nostra pace": among the most quoted lines in the poem. The sea that follows answers the "great sea of being" of Canto 1: every creature sails toward God's will as rivers run to the sea.
Dante sees it now: every soul in Heaven is completely happy, though not all receive the same measure of grace. Each is filled to its own capacity and wants no more.
A weaver's image. Her vow is a cloth left unfinished on the loom, and Dante asks what it was.

context: Piccarda joined her order, the Poor Clares, in Florence.

note: Christ. A nun was called a bride of Christ, and her vows were her wedding.

quote: men more accustomed to evil than good
note: Her brother Corso Donati and his followers. Corso, later the violent leader of the Black Guelph party in Florence, took her from the convent by force and married her to a political ally, Rossellino della Tosa.

quote: God knows what my life became after
note: She says no more, and the silence is famous. Early commentators report that she fell ill and died soon after the marriage, but that may be legend.
The brightest soul in the moon.

quote: never removed the veil from her heart
note: Inwardly she stayed a nun. Beatrice will test this claim in Canto 4, where it seems to clash with what she says about the will.

context: Dante follows the story that she was taken from a convent to be married. Her grandson Manfred named her with pride in Purgatorio 3.

note: The "winds" of Swabia are the Hohenstaufen emperors, whose family came from Swabia in southern Germany: mighty and soon over, like storms. The first was Frederick Barbarossa. The second was his son Henry VI, Constance's husband.

context: Constance's son, the last of his house to hold the empire.

note: "Hail Mary", the angel Gabriel's greeting to the Virgin (Luke 1) and the best known prayer to her. It suits a woman who vowed her virginity to God.

quote: like something heavy through deep water
note: She fades as she appeared, like a face seen in water, sinking back into the pearl of the moon.
Beatrice grows more radiant with every heaven they climb, and each time Dante's eyes must grow strong enough to bear her.
